meta.title: My game collection as code, on Omarchy
meta.description: How I use AI agents to keep Steam games, emulators, PC ports and decomps in an idempotent Ansible repo inside a distrobox, with my own Omarchy launcher.

hero.title: Not everything is work. Even I need to play.
hero.lede: And my idea of relaxing is, of course, turning my game collection into a software project. Steam games, emulators, PC ports, decompilations, fan games and mod packs, all installed, configured and documented by AI agents in one Ansible repository. It runs inside a container, so my Omarchy desktop never sees a single one of their dependencies. On top sits a launcher I wrote, so the whole thing feels like a console.
hero.shotAlt: My games launcher on Omarchy: a fullscreen grid of 52 game covers including Banjo-Kazooie Recompiled, OutRun, the Colin McRae Rally series, Donkey Kong Country and DOOM 3, with category chips and sort buttons on top.
hero.caption: The launcher on my desktop: every game, port and emulator in one grid, whatever it runs on underneath.

drive.title: Fun to Drive: the new Tesla Roadster in an 80s arcade racer
drive.lede: A small game I vibe coded with AI agents. The newly announced Tesla Roadster, cold-air thruster and jump kick included, races down an Outrun-style road on the screen of an 80s toy dashboard, like the Playmates Fun-to-Drive and Tectoy's Turbo Video Driver.
points: Pick a two, six or ten minute run and pass as much traffic as you can before time runs out. Each run starts in the season and time of day of your own clock.
Collect three cold-air charges to fire the thruster, and Jump Kicks to leap over traffic, unless you land on it.
The toy reacts on the desk: the wheel turns, the gear lever moves, and the whole dashboard jolts when you crash.

Clear skies, rain and snow, seasonal scenery from sakura to bare winter trees, and backdrops from Tokyo neon to Paris. Watch for the rare ones: a hurricane that lifts traffic, a UFO abduction at night and, if you hold 88 mph, a time machine.
Play with a keyboard, a gamepad with rumble, or touch. It runs in the browser, written in Rust with Bevy and compiled to WebAssembly.
drive.videoLabel: A 2:20 playthrough of Fun to Drive, with sound
drive.caption: A full playthrough, with the game's own music.

launchers.title: Old racing games, playable again
launchers.lede: Some of my favorite racing games are abandonware: no store sells them, and they won't run on a modern PC without an afternoon of hacks. So I wrote a launcher for each one, with coding agents and my reverse engineering tool, REA. The original game stays untouched. The launcher fixes what aged around it, like graphics, controls, screen and Registry, then adds what a modern PC can do.
launchers.own: You need your own copy of each game. No launcher ships game files.
launchers.post: How I fixed them, on my blog
launchers.note: They are experimental. I tested each one end to end on Linux, with an RTX 5090 and an Xbox-style controller. Only Rad Mobile has been tested on native Windows so far, with a Fanatec wheel, so if you try another one there, open an issue with the executable's SHA-256 and the log.

radmobile.name: Rad Mobile
radmobile.alt: Rad Mobile in true widescreen: Las Vegas at night, seen from behind the wheel, with the casinos drawn past the original 4:3 edges.
radmobile.was: Sega's 1990 arcade game. MAME runs it, but a modern wheel has to turn to full lock before the car does, there is no force feedback, a gamepad stick keeps the car turning after you let go, and the picture is 4:3.
adds: Reads your wheel itself, scaled to the cabinet's 270° steering lock
Force feedback the cabinet never had, made from the running game
Assisted stick steering for gamepads
True widescreen up to 4K, CRT filters and a cabinet bezel

screamer.name: Screamer trilogy
screamer.alt: Screamer on a modern PC: a red sports car racing down a city street, with the original lap counter and speedometer.
screamer.was: Three MS-DOS games. GOG's Screamer 2 ships a Windows Glide stub that doesn't work in DOS, and at full emulator speed the analog controls never register.
adds: Real 3dfx Glide, with the emulated Voodoo drawing at twice the resolution
FSR upscaling, Hor+ widescreen and a longer draw distance
Analog controls and CD music
Experimental frame generation at 100 fps

cmr1.name: Colin McRae Rally
cmr1.alt: Colin McRae Rally from 1998 in widescreen: the blue Subaru on a dry gravel stage.
cmr1.was: Made for Windows 95. On my machine it took Registry keys, XP compatibility mode, a screen locked at 800x600 and a keyboard bridge for the gamepad, and it still ran at 800x600 in 4:3.
adds: 4K, Hor+ widescreen and 60 fps, with the original 25 Hz physics
HD art redrawn with AI for the HUD, menus, skies, signs and cars
Up to three times the draw distance
Triggers as pedals, and rumble

initiald.name: Initial D Arcade series
initiald.alt: Initial D THE ARCADE Season 5: a Trueno racing up a dark mountain road at night.
initiald.was: Eleven arcade games, from 2002 to 2025. TeknoParrot, the usual way to play them, is a Windows .NET program with a closed core and paid tiers. With the open loaders, Initial D 4 crashed at the start of every game and Zero never left its calibration screen.
adds: Open loaders only, with fixes for Initial D 4 and Zero
One hub for the whole series, on Linux and Windows
Wheel and pad support for every game
Up to 4K, with FSR 1 and NVIDIA Image Scaling on Linux

cmr3.name: Colin McRae Rally 3
cmr3.alt: Colin McRae Rally 3 in widescreen: the Ford Focus on a forest stage.
cmr3.was: A washed-out picture, and an official 1.1 executable tied to disc copy protection.
adds: SilentPatch widescreen at any aspect ratio, with an HD interface in 4K
Converts the 1.1 executable into the re-releases' DRM-free one
Anisotropic filtering up to 16x and an adjustable field of view
An optional color and gamma fix on Linux

cmr4.name: Colin McRae Rally 04
cmr4.alt: Colin McRae Rally 04 in 16:9: a Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution on a dusty hillside stage.
cmr4.was: 16:9 shows no extra scenery, the graphics menu stops at 2048x1536 and crashes, and Alt+F4 does nothing.
adds: 16:9 with the right geometry, through dgVoodoo
Picks the landscape monitor, and closing the window works
Analog triggers and a controller that comes configured
Optional fps cap and vsync

cmr2005.name: Colin McRae Rally 2005
cmr2005.alt: Colin McRae Rally 2005 in 16:9: a blue Subaru on a forest stage.
cmr2005.was: Crashes at launch under Wine, and GOG's installer hangs there. The DVD editions use StarForce and aren't supported.
adds: Installs straight from GOG's installer files
16:9 with the game's own wide view
DXVK on Linux: a stage that ran at about 20 fps now passes 1,000
Saves in their own folder

outrun.name: OutRun 2006: Coast 2 Coast
outrun.alt: OutRun 2006 in 4K: a silver convertible on a coastal city highway.
outrun.was: The PC port needs community fixes and its disc DRM removed, and it lost the first two seconds of "Rush a Difficulty".
adds: OutRun2006Tweaks installed for you, at a fixed, tested version
4K, 16x anisotropic filtering and a longer draw distance
The full "Rush a Difficulty"
Optional HD textures, rumble and full triggers

dirt.name: Colin McRae: DiRT
dirt.alt: Colin McRae: DiRT: a rally car kicking up dust on a gravel road through the forest.
dirt.was: Crashes loading any race on a CPU with many threads, and the community fix resets every graphics setting.
adds: Its own fix for the many-thread crash, with your settings kept
Large Address Aware, so the game can use more than 2 GB
Hard links instead of a second copy of 9 GB
The Ultra preset in 4K, and native XInput

srr.name: Sega Rally Revo
srr.alt: Sega Rally Revo: a red Citroën leading the pack on a muddy jungle track.
srr.was: A constant microstutter from two timing bugs in patch 4.060, a black screen on PCs with two GPUs, and a settings tool that fails under Wine.
adds: A clean-room stutter fix: the race clock stays within 1 ms of real time in 99.9% of frames
4K, Ultra quality, 21:9 and 32:9
A 60 or 120 fps cap
Native XInput and rumble

wangan.name: Wangan Midnight series
wangan.alt: Wangan Midnight Maximum Tune 3DX+ drawn at 4K: a silver sports car on a walled expressway.
wangan.was: TeknoParrot's window doubles as the cabinet's I/O board, so it has to stay open while you play, and the loader for 6 and 6RR is closed. Under Wine, the 5 and 6 games crashed on their first movie, and 6RR stopped at its boot checks.
adds: Its own I/O board, so no TeknoParrot and no .NET
Fixes for Maximum Tune 6 and 6RR, and movies that play under Wine
Maximum Tune 3 and 3DX+ drawn natively at up to 4K
One hub and one input path for pads and wheels

dirtrally.name: DiRT Rally
dirtrally.alt: DiRT Rally in full screen: a red Mini on a rocky mountain road.
dirtrally.was: Feral's 2017 Linux port crashes at launch on Ryzen 5000 and newer, needs libraries modern Linux dropped, and was pulled from sale in 2022.
adds: A small Rust library fixes the crash without touching the game
Brings the old libraries, for the game only
Skips Feral's pre-launch window and opens in 4K
Controllers like 8BitDo's show up in the game's own list

sdk.title: Then the recipe became an SDK
sdk.lede: Each launcher started as a copy of the last one, and every copy drifted with its own bugs. So I did what I always tell people to do: build the apps first, then extract the framework. rea-launcher-sdk holds what the launchers share, and it is written for a coding agent to drive.
steps: Build several projects of the same kind, each one solving its real problem.
Refactor until they all stand on the same foundation.
Only then extract the common parts into a framework.

stats.launchers: launchers built on it, for {games} games
stats.tests: tests across the SDK and the launchers, all passing
stats.coverage: line coverage of the SDK's own code, {tests} tests
stats.hours: hours for each launcher made from the SDK, against 8 to 18 before it

sdk.howTitle: Make a launcher for your own game
sdk.how: Clone the SDK, add REA to your agent, and point it at your installed game. The agent researches the community fixes, does the reverse engineering and writes the code. It stops at four checkpoints for your decisions and publishes nothing without your approval. It works with Claude Code, Codex, opencode or Cursor.
sdk.prompt: Create a new rea launcher for Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed (PC, 2000) using the SDK in ~/Projects/rea-launcher-sdk. Read AGENTS.md, docs/STANDARDS.md and docs/playbooks/new-launcher.md and follow the playbook phase by phase. The game is installed in /mnt/games/NFSPU (read only, never copy it into the repo). Research community fixes first and show me what you found before writing code. Don't push or publish anything without asking me.
sdk.promptNote: An example prompt, adapted from the SDK's README.

clean.title: The host stays clean
clean.lede: Emulators and Windows games drag in 32-bit libraries, Wine builds, AUR packages and runtime versions that fight each other. None of that touches my desktop. It all lives in one Arch Linux distrobox called gaming, Steam included, and the host keeps only what the desktop needs.
clean.alt: Two panels. Without a container: a Host tower buried under a tangle of library blocks with red Conflicts warnings. With distrobox: the same Host clean with a green dot, and next to it an orange gaming container holding the same blocks in tidy rows, with an Ansible recipe labelled Rebuild anytime.
points: Steam runs inside the box, with my library and its Proton prefixes on their own disk
The NVIDIA driver is passed through, and the one 32-bit library edge case is fixed in the launcher, never on the host
The box renders desktop entries; a small host script validates and installs them, and removes the ones for apps that are gone
Saves are mirrored to my NAS and restored on demand, so wiping the box loses nothing

idempotent.title: Idempotent, so I can break it
idempotent.lede: Every emulator, config, patch and mod set is an Ansible role. Running the playbook a second time changes nothing, so I can experiment freely, reset a single emulator's settings, or rebuild the whole box from scratch and get the same machine back.
idempotent.docs: notes in docs/, one per game, port or fix

research.title: AI does the research, and writes it down
research.lede: For every port, recompilation or stubborn Windows game, an agent researched the sources, wrote the Ansible role and left a note with where to get it, how it is set up and what did not work. Steam games have their own compatibility database under Proton, with each local fix backed by a source.

items.title: Emulators
items.text: ES-DE as the frontend, plus standalone shadPS4, Dolphin, PCSX2, DuckStation, Flycast, xemu, RPCS3, PPSSPP, Azahar, Eden, Cemu, Supermodel and RetroArch with its cores.

items.title: Ports, decomps and recomps
items.text: Native builds such as Ship of Harkinian, 2Ship2Harkinian, Starship, SpaghettiKart, Render96ex and Unleashed Recompiled.

items.title: Windows games
items.text: Wine-managed installs and fixes for games like the Metal Gear Master Collection. The old racing games now come in through my own launchers, above.

items.title: Mods, reproducibly
items.text: NexusMods mod sets per game, DLC and patch installers for PS3 and Switch, and per-game RPCS3 settings.

menu.title: My own launcher, made for Omarchy
menu.lede: omarchy-games-menu is a Steam-like fullscreen launcher for Omarchy and Hyprland. It reads the desktop entries the gaming repository exports, so a new game shows up by itself, and it puts everything a keybinding away.
menu.alt: Three layers: a Host slab, an orange distrobox container labelled gaming holding Emulators and PC ports with an Ansible recipe, and a Launcher grid of cover art on top.
points: A Rust CLI, ogm, does the scanning, catalog and persistence; a QuickShell overlay draws the grid
Cover art and metadata from SteamGridDB, and new-release checks on GitHub for ports and recomps
Sorted by most played, name, date added or release date; type anywhere to filter
Scales with Hyprland's monitor setting, opens with one key such as Super+G, and games open fullscreen on a dedicated workspace

note.title: Why it is on this site
note.text: Both repositories were written with the same agents and skills as everything else here. They are the clearest example I have of the rule I apply everywhere: if a machine's setup is not code, it is not documented, and if it is not documented, it will break the day you need it.

use.title: How to use it
use.lede: The easiest way is to let an agent do it. Clone the repository, open Claude Code inside it, and tell it which container and games you want. The playbooks and notes are written for exactly that.
use.prompt: Set up the gaming container with ES-DE, Dolphin and PCSX2. My ROMs and BIOS files are in /path/to/your/games.
use.note: The repository ships no games, ROMs, BIOS or other binaries. You bring your own and tell the agent where they are.
